analysis.one_liner: Bans price gouging on prescription drugs covered by federal health programs.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate health committee in February 2019 and never received a vote before the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it illegal for drug manufacturers to raise prices on drugs covered by Medicare, Medicaid, and other federal health programs in ways that outstrip real cost increases and that consumers cannot avoid by switching. Price hikes of 10% in a year, 20% in three years, or 30% in five years would be presumed gouging. The Health and Human Services Secretary could then order refunds to consumers and insurers, force the old price for up to a year, and impose civil penalties up to three times the excessive amount.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients and taxpayers who pay for drugs through federal health programs like Medicare and Medicaid, and third-party insurers, would get refunds of excessive price increases and relief from unjustified hikes. Anyone whose prescriptions fall under these programs — which is most people over 65 and many low-income households — would gain a check on sudden, extreme price spikes.

how_it_helps.text: Presumes price gouging when a drug's average manufacturer price rises 10% or more in 12 months, 20% in 36 months, or 30% in 60 months, subject to a manufacturer's written justification.

Lets the Secretary of Health and Human Services order refunds to consumers and third-party payors, require the pre-hike price for up to a year, and impose civil penalties of up to three times the excessive amount for knowing or repeat violations.
Authorizes the Attorney General to enforce Secretary's orders in federal court and to subpoena documents or testimony in price gouging investigations.

analysis.who_pays: Prescription drug manufacturers who raise prices faster than production costs on drugs covered by federal health programs would bear the cost, in refunds, temporary price rollbacks, and penalties. Drug makers as a whole would also lose pricing freedom on this segment of the market, which critics say could reduce the revenue that funds research on new medicines.

drawbacks.text: The 10%-in-12-months presumption is a low trigger that could sweep in price increases that have genuine cost-based justifications, requiring manufacturers to defend ordinary business decisions to the Secretary — though the bill does allow a statement of justification with itemized production costs.
The prohibition covers only drugs covered by federal health care programs, leaving people paying cash or through private insurance without the same protection.

Critics of drug price regulation generally argue that capping or penalizing price increases reduces expected returns and could slow investment in new medicines; the bill does not address this objection.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a targeted anti-gouging measure rather than a broad price control: it only penalizes hikes presumed excessive and lets manufacturers justify real cost increases. For Medicare and Medicaid patients it offers concrete refunds and a deterrent against spikes like the ones that have drawn national attention. Its main weakness is scope — it leaves privately insured and cash-pay patients out — and a low 10% trigger that may be overbroad, though the justification process softens that.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, where it sat without a hearing, markup, or floor vote until the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Senator Richard Blumenthal introduced the CURE High Drug Prices Act on February 28, 2019, with five cosponsors: Senators Merkley, Harris, Klobuchar, Schatz, and Sanders.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the same day; that referral was the last action of any kind in its two-year history.
The bill never received a committee vote, a hearing recorded in its action history, or a Senate floor vote before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Prescription drug manufacturers are better off: they face none of the bill's refund requirements, price rollbacks, or civil penalties for large price increases on drugs covered by federal health programs. Patients on those programs saw no change.

for.name: Sen. Richard Blumenthal
for.role: U.S. Senator from Connecticut; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the CURE High Drug Prices Act on February 28, 2019.

for.name: Sens. Merkley, Harris, Klobuchar, Schatz, and Sanders
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; no Republican signed on.

against.role: Chair of the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing, markup, or vote after it was referred to the committee on February 28, 2019.

sides.party_line_note: All six sponsors were Democrats or an Independent aligned with them; no Republican cosponsored, and the bill died in a committee chaired by a Republican without any recorded votes.

industries.note: The bill would require refunds of excessive price increases on drugs covered by Medicare, Medicaid, and other federal programs, plus civil penalties up to three times the excessive amount for knowing or repeat gouging. Their gain from large price hikes that patients cannot avoid is directly what the bill targets.

industries.industry: Third-party payors (insurers and pharmacy benefit plans)
industries.note: They would be eligible for restitution of excessive amounts paid as a result of gouging, sharing the bill's protection with patients.
